description: We are three teenagers from Málaga passionate about technology, innovation and solving real-world problems. We work with programming, AI, web development, APIs, data and experimental projects. After participating last year, we are back for the experience, the challenge and the chance to create something useful. This year, we are especially interested in health and in building solutions that can genuinely help people.
summary:
XPaze is a pocket doctor for astronauts, built by Los Zenith for the NASA Space Apps Challenge Málaga 2026 (challenge: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions). On long missions, crews live isolated, sleep badly and are far from any hospital, yet today’s monitors compare everyone against the same fixed thresholds. XPaze learns what is normal for each crew member and warns when they drift from it: 108 bpm after exercise is fine, but 84 at rest in someone who is always at 62 is not.

A station reads pulse, SpO₂ and cabin conditions, a Galaxy Watch adds real pulse and steps through our XPaze Link app, and a phone app shows history, step-by-step guides and a green, amber and red traffic light. The personal baseline (median and MAD, EWMA, Isolation Forest) runs on board with no connection, with NASA-STD-3001 limits as a safety net. NASA’s DONKI space weather data triggers shelter alerts, and Human Research Program risks explain each reading. Paze, our voice psychologist, uses mood, reflexes and sleep to spot exhaustion or stress.

The same approach serves anyone far from a doctor: seafarers, Antarctic crews, remote areas and emergencies. XPaze does not diagnose; it supports doctors. Today we have a working MVP, a physical sensor prototype in testing and a demo with four astronauts at xpaze.es. Next: Paze fully offline, ECG in the station and a test in a real mission analogue.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
XPaze is a pocket doctor for astronauts. It learns what each crew member is normally like, physically and mentally, notices when that changes and explains why, without depending on Earth. Today’s monitors compare everyone against the same fixed thresholds; XPaze compares each person with themselves. 108 bpm after exercise is normal, but 84 at rest in someone who is always at 62 is a warning sign.

The system has three parts:

  • The station: the astronaut taps their ID card and grips the handles to measure pulse and SpO₂. It also logs cabin temperature, humidity and pressure.
  • The watch: a Galaxy Watch adds real pulse and step data through our XPaze Link app.
  • The phone app: it shows the history, step-by-step and emergency guides, and a green, amber or red traffic light.

The personal baseline combines median and MAD, EWMA and Isolation Forest, and it runs on board with no connection. NASA-STD-3001 limits act as a safety net. The server also checks NASA’s DONKI space weather data every 3 hours and triggers a shelter alert when there is a solar radiation warning.

Paze, our voice psychologist, crosses mood, reflexes and sleep with physical data to spot exhaustion or stress.

What are the benefits?

  • It detects changes before they become a problem.
  • It explains every alert instead of just showing a number.
  • It guides what to do in each case, including emergencies.
  • It works without a link to Earth.
  • It supports the onboard doctor, who cannot watch everyone around the clock.
  • It protects privacy: the doctor only sees an overall traffic light unless the astronaut chooses to share more.

What is the intended impact?
On lunar and Mars missions, communication delays and blackouts make medical autonomy essential. The same approach works on Earth for anyone far from a doctor: 1.89 million seafarers, over a thousand people wintering in Antarctica, isolated rural areas and emergency situations.

What tools did we use?

  • Hardware: a station with an ID card reader, a pulse and SpO₂ sensor and cabin sensors, built on [Arduino / Raspberry Pi, confirm]. Plus a Galaxy Watch.
    • NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 2 and the OCHMO Technical Briefs for cabin thresholds.
    • DONKI (NASA CCMC) for live space weather.
    • The Human Research Program, to link each measurement to an official risk.
    • The PVT-B reaction test, with a 355 ms lapse threshold.
    • MSL/RAD data for the simulated dosimeter.
    • OSDR (Environmental Data App and OSD-569, Inspiration4) as reference and inspiration.
    • JPL Horizons, to verify the Earth–Mars delay shown on the website.
  • AI: Paze’s voice currently uses a cloud AI model [name]. All AI use is declared in AI_USE.md.

How is it creative?
Instead of asking “is this number high?”, XPaze asks “is this number normal for this person, right now?”. It reads body and mind together, since a bad night shows up both in the pulse and in mood. It also turns NASA standards and live space weather into clear actions, and it gives psychological support a voice through Paze, who remembers past sessions and each astronaut’s real data.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Autonomy: baseline and alerts work fully offline.
  • Safety: NASA’s fixed limits always remain as a backstop.
  • Honesty: XPaze does not diagnose, is not a medical device and never replaces doctors.
  • Privacy: astronauts decide what they share.
  • Usability: measuring takes a single gesture at the station, and every alert explains itself.
  • Current limits: Paze still needs the cloud, and the physical prototype is still being validated with real sensors. Our next steps are running Paze fully offline, adding ECG and body temperature to the station, and testing XPaze in a real mission analogue.
dataRefs: NASA DONKI – Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information (CCMC)
NASA/JPL Horizons System – solar system ephemerides
NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 2 – OCHMO Technical Brief: ECLSS (cabin temperature, humidity, pressure)
NASA Human Research Program – Human Research Roadmap: Risks
NASA OSDR – Environmental Data App (ISS cabin data)
NASA MSL/RAD – Zeitlin et al., Science 2013 (radiation in transit to Mars)
projectRefs: NEWS2 – National Early Warning Score 2 (Royal College of Physicians)
PVT-B – Basner, Mollicone & Dinges, Acta Astronautica 2011
AHA/ACCF/HRS ECG standardization, Part IV (QT interval)
Drew et al. – Prevention of Torsade de Pointes, Circulation 2010
Overbey et al. – SOMA / Inspiration4, Nature 632 (2024)
ESConv – Emotional Support Conversation dataset (strategy taxonomy)
Anthropic Claude API (check-up explanation and Paze text) and Claude Code (development)
OpenAI Realtime API (Paze live voice) and OpenAI Codex (development)
Android Health Connect (Galaxy Watch data via XPaze Link)
